channel.title: LangMap Sinosphere
channel.description: Short stories about Han characters, words and sounds across China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam, first posted to the SINOSPHERE 漢字文化圈 Facebook group.

item.title: Bubble Tea: Pearls, Bubbles, and a Hong Kong Actress
item.description: In Taiwan, the little balls in milk tea became "pearls." In English, the drink became "bubble tea," a name whose bubbles may never have been bubbles at all. And in America, it became "boba," a word with a cheeky history, a Hong Kong actress, and an English word hidden inside.

item.title: Yesterday and Tomorrow: What If They Were the Same Word?
item.description: In Hindi, "yesterday" and "tomorrow" are exactly the same word. In Japanese, "tomorrow" once meant "morning." Surprisingly, English and several European languages did something similar. And in Korea, an ancient Chinese book preserves a forgotten native word for tomorrow.

item.title: Four Places, One Name: 板橋
item.description: Tokyo has a district called 板橋, pronounced Itabashi. The same characters appear in Pangyo, Korea, and Banqiao in both Nanjing and New Taipei. All four names tell stories of wooden bridges. But are they really just coincidences?

item.title: Butter: One Food, Many Histories
item.description: In Japan and Korea, butter sounds English. In Vietnam, it sounds French. In the Philippines, it sounds Spanish. In Chinese, the same butter can be called "yellow oil," "cow oil," or "milk oil," depending on where you are. But thousands of years before these modern names, butter already had a place in the religions and cultures of Asia.

item.title: Dragon Mountain: 龍山 Across East Asia
item.description: Seoul has a place called 龍山, the Dragon Mountain. China has another 龍山, a name that became famous in archaeology. Japan has one too. But its dragon has a rather unexpected origin.

item.title: How to Turn Bad Luck into Good Luck, Just by Changing a Word
item.description: In Japan, a squid that sounded like losing money became a winning squid. In Cantonese, a vegetable that suggested defeat was renamed "Victory Melon." In Thailand, a flower escaped sorrow, and a bankrupt dessert turned into gold.

item.title: Thank You: One Feeling, Many Hidden Stories
item.description: In Japanese, "thank you" originally described something almost impossible to find. In Cantonese, a gift and a glass of water call for different kinds of thanks. And two Chinese characters traveled all the way to Indonesia, even reaching people who never learned to write them.

item.title: Three Lakes, One Name: 西湖
item.description: China, Vietnam and Japan each have a famous lake called 西湖, "West Lake". The same two characters are read Xīhú in Hangzhou, Tây Hồ in Hanoi and Saiko at the foot of Mount Fuji. Behind the one name lie three different histories, and a legend that may be younger than it looks.

item.title: China's Space Program: Where Technology Meets Poetry
item.description: China builds rockets, space stations, lunar landers, and planetary probes using some of the world's most advanced technology. Yet their names come from ancient goddesses, legendary bridges, classical poetry, and questions asked thousands of years ago. The further China reaches into space, the more poetic its spacecraft names seem to become.

item.title: Wisdom, Love, and Missing Parents: What East Asia Calls the Wisdom Tooth
item.description: In China and Vietnam, the last molar is a symbol of wisdom. In Korea, it is the "tooth of love," arriving around the time of first romance. But in Japan, it is the "tooth that doesn't know its parents." And in ancient China, one doctor was beaten for telling the truth about it.

item.title: Biáng: 58 Strokes for a Bowl of Noodles
item.description: In Xi'an, China, a humble bowl of noodles has a name written with one of the most complicated Chinese characters in everyday use. Its traditional form has 58 strokes, combining horses, hearts, moons, and other familiar characters into one extraordinary symbol. For years, computers couldn't properly handle it. Only in 2020 did the character finally receive an official place in Unicode.

item.title: One to Ten: When Numbers Mean More Than Numbers
item.description: The same ten Chinese characters are pronounced differently across East Asia, preserving centuries of linguistic history. But some numbers carry meanings far beyond arithmetic. One can change its name. Four can bring bad luck. And eight can be worth a fortune.

item.title: What does your language call China?
item.description: Some languages call it by its own name. Some may remember an empire from more than 2,000 years ago. Others still call it by the name of a people who ruled northern China around 1,000 years ago.

item.title: The Secret Life of 99 (Part 3): When Ninety Means Four and a Half Twenties
item.description: French expresses 99 as "four twenties plus nineteen." But twenty-based counting is far from unusual in Europe. Basque, Welsh, Breton, and Danish preserve different versions of this system. Danish even expresses ninety through an ancient formula involving four and a half twenties. Thousands of years earlier, Mesopotamian civilizations developed counting based on sixty, leaving traces in the clocks we use today.

item.title: The Secret Life of 99 (Part 2): When Ten Is Not Always Ten
item.description: Vietnamese preserves two traditions of counting, one native and one Chinese-derived. Even a group called "ten" may not always contain exactly ten items. Thai numbers sound surprisingly similar to Cantonese, preserving traces of ancient connections with Chinese. In Khmer, nine is literally "five plus four." And 99 combines two different histories in a single expression.

item.title: The Secret Life of 99 (Part 1): A Number Hidden in an Ancient Manuscript
item.description: In Chinese, 99 is simply "nine-ten-nine." But even Chinese has surprising exceptions to its regular counting system. In Japan, the same three characters, 九十九, can become a poetic image of old age. In Korea, native words for the tens survive today, and a Chinese manuscript recorded them more than 900 years ago, long before Hangul existed.

item.title: Why does "Ri" become "I" in South Korean names?
item.description: The Chinese character 李 is read "ri" in Korean. But in South Korea, it becomes "i" at the beginning of a name. In North Korea, the "r" stays. Why?

item.title: Why does Asia have so many different names for Germany?
item.description: Japan says Doitsu. China says Déguó. South Korea says Dogil. Same country, so why are the names so different? Because two different Chinese characters, 獨 and 德, took two different routes across East Asia.

item.title: Why does so much of the world call goosebumps "bird skin"?
item.description: Japanese has a strange expression for goosebumps. It calls them "bird skin." Then you look next door, and the neighbors see poultry too. Then you look at Europe, and things start getting suspicious.

item.title: What if English had invented its own Chinese characters?
item.description: Imagine writing man, eat and dog with Chinese-style characters. It sounds like a strange experiment. But across parts of Asia, languages really did something remarkably similar.

item.title: What do you call a computer?
item.description: When computers arrived in Asia, many languages simply borrowed the English word computer. Others translated what the machine did. And a few gave it a completely new metaphor.

item.title: Why does so much of Asia count things this way?
item.description: Chinese, Vietnamese, Korean and Japanese are not one language family. Yet all four make you choose special words when you count things. And once you look across Asia, the pattern becomes hard to explain as coincidence.

item.title: Why is 西瓜 pronounced suika?
item.description: Japan has a very ordinary word with a surprisingly strange pronunciation. The word is 西瓜, "watermelon", read suika. Look closely at the first character, and you find three layers of borrowed Chinese.

item.title: One Dragon, Five Languages
item.description: Hanoi was once called Thăng Long, 昇龍, "Ascending Dragon." Japanese ryū, Mandarin lóng, Cantonese lung, Korean yong, Vietnamese long. Five languages that cannot understand one another, yet the family resemblance is still easy to hear.

item.title: 口, 嘴, 喙: When a Beak Becomes a Mouth
item.description: The character 口 looks like the obvious way to write "mouth." But across Chinese varieties, it is actually only one of several everyday choices. Two of the most common alternatives, 嘴 and 喙, both have old associations with a beak or snout.

item.title: When a Polite "You" Becomes Rude
item.description: Japanese お前 (omae) and 貴様 (kisama) can sound rough or openly hostile today. But both began in strongly respectful language. Korean and Chinese show similar changes too, although usually not as dramatically as Japanese.

item.title: Seven Characters, Seven Days: 月火水木金土日
item.description: Japanese and Korean use the same seven characters for the days of the week: 月火水木金土日. The seven-day planetary week came to East Asia from the west, but China gave the five planets their familiar 五行 names. Japan and Korea kept those old names, while modern China and Vietnam chose different systems.

item.title: I Know the Characters. But Not That Meaning. Part 4: New Lives for Familiar Characters
item.description: In Chinese, 老婆 is an ordinary word for "wife"; in Japanese and Korean, the same characters mean "elderly woman." Words like 爱人, 结束, 检讨, 工夫 and 经理 split their meanings differently across Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese. Chinese itself keeps coining new words from old characters, from 充电宝 to 智商税 and 负豪.

item.title: I Know the Characters. But Not That Meaning. Part 3: "Are You Okay?" Written 大丈夫
item.description: In Japanese, 大丈夫 (daijōbu) means "okay"; in Chinese, 大丈夫 is still a principled, resolute man. 我慢, 達者, 挨拶, 喧嘩 and 贔屓 all mean something different in everyday Japanese from what a Chinese reader might expect. This is not just old vocabulary preserved in Japan, but a record of words changing through use.

item.title: I Know the Characters. But Not That Meaning. Part 2: An Office Called 文房
item.description: A Vietnamese university student is a sinh viên, written 生員, a name once tied to the imperial examinations. A watch is đồng hồ (銅壺), an office is văn phòng (文房), and a writer's fee is nhuận bút (潤筆). Read through their older associations, these words describe a scholar's life; read as Vietnamese, they describe a modern one.
